title: Unsigned acts land dream Peter Gabriel studio session
content:
For most aspiring musicians, spending four days recording in a world-famous studio would be out of reach.
But seven unsigned acts from across the West Country have been given that opportunity after being selected from more than 400 applicants to record at Peter Gabriel's renowned Real World Studios in Wiltshire.
The artists will follow in the footsteps of acts including Harry Styles, Coldplay and Amy Winehouse after being chosen by a panel of industry experts as part of a scheme funded through a partnership between Real World and Arts Council England.
"It's a huge privilege," said Luca Williamson, drummer with Bristol band 1000 Legs. "These places are so hard to access."
For many of the musicians, it is their first time recording in a professional studio.
By the end of the programme, each act will leave with a fully mixed and mastered EP.
The opportunity comes at a time when many emerging artists are balancing music with work, study and rising living costs.
"Most of us are students, working hospitality jobs at the same time as well as trying to pay the rent," said saxophonist Gabriel Bonner-Thomas, of 1000 Legs.
"It's hard on time and money, so you have to be so passionate about it. Over the course of a month it could be £60 each just to rehearse, there aren't a lot of spaces to do it, it's tough."
The chance to record at Real World would normally be beyond the reach of many unsigned musicians.
"The list of people who've recorded here is really cool, but it's also being in a room which is this acoustically brilliant, with this much amazing gear, and recording to tape is something we'd never be able to afford," said guitarist Jerome Gamlin.
Bassist Ben Lefever added: "It is very different, because a lot of the time when you practice you are so focused on your own instrument, but when you get in here, such a high-class studio, you get to hear everything played back at you in the way it's intended to be heard."
Guitarist Cass Dener said opportunities like this could make a significant difference to artists outside major music hubs.
"So much talent goes unnoticed because of location, people who live in small towns without venues, so for Real World to give this opportunity is a lovely thing," he said.
Another artist who has been chosen to record at Real World Studios  - singing in the same space as Beyoncé, Björk and Alicia Keys - is Bristol vocalist Aloka Collister.
"It took me a whole day to accept I'm actually doing this," said the 23-year-old.
"It feels cosmic, this thing I could only have ever dreamed of is happening in my reality, I'm very emotional," she added.
Collister said music had helped her through difficult periods in her life.
"I struggle with depression, I struggle to leave the house sometimes," she said.
"Singing is baring your heart and soul, sometimes I've been on stage in a vulnerable state. Music makes me feel free.

final_quality.reason: This article reports on a unique opportunity for unsigned musicians in the West Country to record at Peter Gabriel's renowned Real World Studios, a significant development for the entertainment category that provides insight into the challenges faced by emerging artists and the impact of such opportunities on their careers.

title: BBC and Netflix team up for new CBeebies hub on streamer
content:
The BBC and Netflix are to launch a trial hub on the streaming service next month, featuring 24 CBeebies shows.
Programmes including Hey Duggee, Numberblocks and Teletubbies can be seen on a branded CBeebies hub on Netflix from 2 December.
The trial's aim is to test new ways for the flagship pre-school channel to reach audiences. The BBC is the UK's largest commissioner of children's content.
BBC iPlayer will remain the home for all CBeebies content. Some CBeebies shows such as Shaun the Sheep are already available on Netflix, but this is the first time they will have a home hub on the subscription streamer.
CBeebies shows will also be made available to Netflix members outside the UK in a distribution deal managed by BBC Studios, with the aim of driving investment into children's content in the UK. The deal does not include China.
Netflix will also commit to funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions, the BBC said.
BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips said the corporation is "always looking at how we can help more audiences discover" its content and brands.
"This limited trial will make a curated selection of CBeebies programmes available on Netflix, while BBC iPlayer remains the home of the full CBeebies experience," she added.
Anne Mensah, vice president of Netflix's UK content said the "unique partnership allows us to work hand in hand with the BBC to support our brilliant British kids' programme makers".
She added: "We want to build a fun and safe space parents can feel good about, with content their kids will love."
The news comes against the backdrop of big changes at the BBC.
The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach a £500m savings target.
The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.
The corporation also faces growing competition for audiences from streaming services, gaming, social media and YouTube.
ranking_reason: The BBC and Netflix team up for a new CBeebies hub on Netflix, a significant development in the entertainment industry.

analysis.reason: The BBC and Netflix team up for a new CBeebies hub on Netflix, a significant development in the entertainment industry.

final_quality.reason: Significant development in the entertainment industry, as the BBC and Netflix team up to launch a new CBeebies hub on Netflix, with a curated selection of 24 shows and a commitment to funding new CBeebies commissions, marking a major expansion of the BBC's reach and presence in the streaming market.

title: First Children's Booker prize reveals shortlist - and its child judges
content:
The first ever Children's Booker Prize has announced the eight books in the running for the new £50,000 award.
Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories are on the shortlist, which is aimed at children aged eight to 12.
The authors in contention include former Children's Laureate of Ireland Eoin Colfer, who is best known for his Artemis Fowl series, and teacher and children's author Catherine Bruton.
Four children have also been announced as new judges after a UK-wide competition. Twelve-year-old Ibrahim from Hampshire was one of those picked from more than 4,000 entrants.
He told me he was called back into school for a phone call with chair of judges Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who broke the news. Ibrahim said he couldn't be happier.
"First Children's Booker Prize judge! On my CV - that's going to take me a long way… I'm too overwhelmed to even be excited."
Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC "it's really, really important that this is a prize for children's books. Having judges who are children will be proof of that… If the children don't love a book, it won't win."
Ibrahim, his fellow child judges and Cottrell-Boyce will be joined on the judging panel by Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, who owns an award-winning children's book shop in north London.
Ibrahim said he loves reading "because it's just a way to unwind yourself from the outside world. If you get stuck in a book, you're not getting your face out of there until you finish it".
He's far too professional to share which books on the list he likes best, but he told me when he was reading one of them recently: "I had to tell my mum to confiscate it because I couldn't stop reading it and I was getting a headache."
Cottrell-Boyce said he isn't concerned over whether the adult judges might dominate the decision-making.
"If - like me - you've been visiting schools as a children's writer for 20 years, it's a rare thing to meet a child who is too over-awed to express an opinion. They're usually very forthright".
Ibrahim proves that point. He told me "the adults are not going to control that meeting… 100% not!"
He's looking for "something that has different perspectives, you can see it in a different way. New characters, not just the same old sloppy characters that authors make all the time. They just make these books that just have the same plot line".
The shortlisted books are by authors and illustrators from the UK, Ireland, Australia and Italy. Cottrell-Boyce described the list as "full of surprises." Here it is:
Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC the range of subjects was "amazing".
"Children's books can be about anything, can deal with anything. But the tone has to convey hope. I can't think of a darker childhood than the one endured by Anne of Green Gables. I also can't think of a more joyous book than Anne of Green Gables."
He acknowledges the worrying statistics on reading. The National Literacy Trust's Annual Literacy Survey last year showed the percentage of children and young people who said they enjoyed reading was its lowest in 20 years. Just one in three aged eight to 18 said they enjoyed reading in their free time, down by more than a third since 2005.
ranking_reason: The announcement of the first Children's Booker Prize and the selection of child judges adds a fresh and unique perspective to the literary world.

analysis.reason: The announcement of the first Children's Booker Prize and the selection of child judges adds a fresh and unique perspective to the literary world.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a unique and significant development in the literary world, the introduction of child judges in a major book award, which provides a fresh perspective and adds to the public interest in the category.
